title: Karnataka Ships First Air Cargo of Totapuri and Neelam Mangoes to Maldives
excerpt: APEDA-backed initiative sources late-season mango varieties from Kolar's farmer-producer company, delivering 50% higher returns to growers and extending India's export window.
body:
• APEDA has flagged off the first air shipment of Totapuri and Neelam mangoes from Karnataka's Kolar district to the Maldives, sourced from the Prakruthimaya Farmer Producer Company.
  • The export, led by a woman entrepreneur, has yielded approximately 50% higher returns for farmers compared to conventional domestic markets.
  • The late-season varieties extend India's mango export window beyond the traditional April-June peak, opening new market opportunities in the Indian Ocean region.

The Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA), under the Union Ministry of Commerce and Industry, has shipped the first air consignment of Totapuri and Neelam mangoes from Karnataka's Kolar district to the Maldives. The shipment, led by a woman entrepreneur, was sourced from the Prakruthimaya Farmer Producer Company (FPC) in Kolar, a district whose Srinivaspura town is often referred to as India's Mango City.

The initiative has delivered approximately 50% higher returns for participating farmers compared to sales in conventional domestic markets, according to APEDA. Both Totapuri and Neelam are late-season mango varieties, and their export helps extend India's mango shipment calendar beyond the traditional peak season that runs from April through June.

Kolar's Mango Heritage

Kolar district, and Srinivaspura in particular, sits at the heart of Karnataka's mango economy. The region boasts over 63 mango varieties, with Totapuri leading production. Srinivaspura's mango market handles roughly 600,000 quintals of fruit annually, making it one of Asia's largest.

Totapuri — named for its distinctive parrot-beak shape (gini meaning parrot, muthi meaning beak in Kannada) — is one of South India's most commercially significant cultivars, accounting for nearly half the mango acreage across the region. Around 80% of Totapuri production is processed into juice, pulp, frozen fruit, and squash, with the remaining 20% consumed fresh. Neelam, smaller in size, is prized for its tangy-sweet flavour and firm, non-fibrous texture, making it a favourite for pickles and chutneys.

Building on a Growing Export Push

The shipment follows a broader pattern of Karnataka-to-Maldives agricultural exports. In January 2026, APEDA facilitated the first-ever air shipment of GI-tagged produce from Karnataka to the Maldives, including Nanjangudu Rasabale bananas, Mysore Betel Leaves, and Indi Lime. That consignment, sourced from farmers in Mysuru and Vijayapura districts, was executed by M/s Silken Global Imports and Exports and endorsed publicly by Union Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal.

Karnataka's mango exports have been on a strong upward trajectory. Kempegowda International Airport (KIAL) in Bengaluru exported 921 metric tonnes of mangoes — equivalent to 31.5 lakh fruits — during the latest season, a 12% increase over the previous year. Shipments from KIAL reached 51 international destinations, with 19 new locations added to the network.

"The success of this mango season speaks of the collaborative efforts of our regulatory bodies, airline partners, cargo handlers, trade promotion councils, trade bodies, and farming communities."

— Satyaki Raghunath, COO, Bangalore International Airport Ltd

Why the Maldives Matters

The Maldives, heavily dependent on food imports, represents a strategic market for Indian horticultural exports. The archipelago's luxury tourism sector drives demand for premium tropical produce, and its proximity to India gives air-shipped fruit a freshness advantage over competing suppliers. Karnataka's mango export data shows the Maldives, alongside Nepal and Bangladesh, among the state's primary export destinations for the fruit.

The involvement of farmer-producer companies like Prakruthimaya FPC is central to the model APEDA is promoting. By linking smallholder growers directly to export channels, the approach aims to cut out intermediaries and ensure a greater share of export premiums reaches the farmgate. The 50% price premium reported in the Maldives shipment echoes results from the January GI-tagged produce export, where banana farmers earned around 50% more and lime growers over 40% above domestic market rates.

What's Next

APEDA's focus on late-season varieties like Totapuri and Neelam signals an effort to stretch India's mango export calendar year-round. The country, which produces roughly 20 million tonnes of mangoes annually — about 45% of global output — has historically exported only a fraction of that volume, with logistics and perishability as key constraints.

Recent breakthroughs in sea-freight protocols, including a successful June 2026 trial shipment of Banganapalle mangoes to Singapore using ICAR-developed shelf-life extension technology, are complementing the air-cargo push. Together, these initiatives aim to make Indian mangoes more competitive in global markets while ensuring that smallholder farmers, not just large exporters, benefit from the growing international appetite for the fruit.
nri_angle: Late-season Totapuri and Neelam mangoes reaching new markets like the Maldives could expand availability of these popular South Indian varieties for overseas Indian communities.
